chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's order. Two games give multiples and factors, primes and co-primes grow out of the factors, and prime factorisation then replaces guessing with one sure method.

points.text: Every word, multiple, common multiple, factor, prime, co-prime, comes from the idli-vada game or Jumpy's treasure jumps before it gets its name.
points.title: Games before definitions

points.text: Each idea gets its own topic: worked videos for the book's examples, one tool to do it by hand, then the book's Figure it Out questions in a practice topic, each with its own video.
points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic

points.text: Writing a number as a product of primes is unique, so it answers two questions without long division: are two numbers co-prime, and does one number divide another.
points.title: One sure method

points.text: Common wrong ideas, such as 'a number ending in 4 can be prime' or 'one factor pair shows every factor', are raised by Keeko and fixed with a picture, never just a rule.
points.title: Keeko's doubts

topics.summary: Two bells, two rhythms: when do they ring together, and why do some pairs of numbers never meet early?

content.text:
1. A temple bell rings every 4 minutes and a school bell every 6 minutes. They ring together at noon.
2. Make a guess before the next step: when will they ring together again?
3. Count the 4s and the 6s. The first time both land on the same minute is 12 minutes later.
4. Some pairs meet quickly, and some, like 5 and 7, meet only at 35. This chapter finds out why.

media.instructions_for_student: Idli is said at multiples of one number, vada at multiples of the other, and idli-vada at the numbers that are both: the common multiples.
media.description:
A ring of children numbered 1 to 60 fills the screen, each one a small round face with the number beside it. Above the ring are two steppers, one for the idli number and one for the vada number, each running from 2 to 12, and a Play button. Beside the ring a tally keeps four counts: just idli, just vada, idli-vada and plain numbers. Before Play is pressed every child is plain and every count is zero.

On each card the student first predicts by typing the first number at which the children will say idli-vada. Then the student sets the two steppers and presses Play, and the game is called round the ring one child at a time. A child who must say idli glows orange, a child who must say vada glows green and a child who must say both glows gold, while the tally counts up. For 3 and 5 the gold children are 15, 30, 45 and 60, and the tally ends at 16 just idli, 8 just vada and 4 idli-vada. Tapping a gold child opens the two skip-counting lists side by side, 3, 6, 9 up to 15 and 5, 10, 15, with the child's number in both, so the student sees that a common multiple is simply a number found in both lists.

The six cards are: idli 3 and vada 5, first idli-vada number (15); idli 4 and vada 6 (12); idli 2 and vada 5 up to 60, how many idli-vada calls (6, at 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60); and idli 3 and vada 7 (21). The last two are open challenges. On the fifth the student chooses two numbers so that nobody ever says just vada, for example idli 4 and vada 8, keeping the vada number as the larger as in the game. The just-vada count stays at zero and every green child is also gold. On the sixth the student chooses two numbers below 10 whose first idli-vada call comes after 50, for example 7 and 8, whose first gold child is 56.

A wrong first number is checked against the glowing children one by one, walking along the ring and stopping at the first gold child, so a student who answers 30 for 3 and 5 sees that 15 came earlier. A solved card lists all the gold numbers as multiples of the first one, which answers the idea that only the first one counts. Hints come in order: which numbers does each child call, read the colours; the idli-vada numbers are the numbers that are in both lists; press Play and look at the first gold number; and last the first gold number is shown with the others following it, and a similar card comes next. Through doing, the student learns that a common multiple is a number in both skip-counting lists, that the first one shows where all the others fall, and that nobody says just vada when the larger number is a multiple of the smaller.

narration: Kiko has one question to ask.
What is the real-life use case?
Two bus routes start together from one Indian bus stand.

content.text:
Children sit in a circle and play a game of numbers.
One of the children starts by saying ‘1’. The second player says ‘2’, and so on. But when it is the turn of 3, 6, 9, … (multiples of 3), the player should say ‘idli’ instead of the number. When it is the turn of 5, 10, … (multiples of 5), the player should say ‘vada’ instead of the number. When a number is both a multiple of 3 and a multiple of 5, the player should say ‘idli-vada’! If a player makes any mistake, they are out.
The game continues in rounds till only one person remains.
For which numbers should the players say ‘idli’ instead of saying the number? These would be 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, … and so on.
For which numbers should the players say ‘vada’? These would be 5, 10, 15, 20, … and so on.

Worked example: Which is the first number for which the players should say ‘idli-vada’? It is 15, a multiple of 3 and also of 5. Find out other such numbers that are multiples of both 3 and 5. These numbers are called ______.
1. Multiples of both 3 and 5 are multiples of 15.
2. The blank is filled by: common multiples.
Answer: 15, 30, 45, 60, … ; they are called common multiples (of 3 and 5)

content.text:
1. Predict first: if one of the numbers is 4, can the other be 8, so that nobody says just vada?
2. Vada is said for multiples of the larger number. Every one must also be a multiple of the smaller.
3. With 4 and 8, every multiple of 8 is also a multiple of 4, so no one says just vada.
4. With 4 and 2 the larger is 4, and every multiple of 4 is a multiple of 2, so that works too.

content.question: Yesterday, we played this game with two numbers. We ended up saying just ‘idli’ or ‘idli-vada’ and nobody said just ‘vada’! One of the numbers was 4. Oh, what could those numbers be!? Which of the following could be the other number: 2, 3, 5, 8, 10?

content.question_tex: Yesterday, we played this game with two numbers. We ended up saying just ‘idli’ or ‘idli-vada’ and nobody said just ‘vada’! One of the numbers was $4$. Oh, what could those numbers be!? Which of the following could be the other number: $2$, $3$, $5$, $8$, $10$?

steps: Vada is said for multiples of the larger number, so every one of them must also be a multiple of the smaller number.
With 4 and 8, every multiple of 8 is a multiple of 4, so nobody says just vada.
With 2 and 4, every multiple of 4 is a multiple of 2, so that works too.
With 3, 5 or 10 someone says just vada: for 3 and 4 it is 4, for 4 and 5 it is 5, for 4 and 10 it is 10.
content.answer: 2 and 8 (the book names only 8).

media.instructions_for_student: A jump size reaches a treasure only if it is a factor of the treasure number, and it reaches two treasures only if it is a common factor.
media.description:
A number line from 0 to 72 stretches across the screen with Jumpy standing at 0. A stepper places one treasure marker on the line, and a second stepper can place a second one. A jump size stepper runs from 1 to 36, and a Jump button moves Jumpy forward by the chosen size each time it is pressed. Every spot where Jumpy lands is marked on the line, and a list called Jump sizes that worked sits beside it, empty at the start.

With one treasure on 24 the student chooses a jump size and presses Jump again and again until Jumpy reaches or passes the treasure. Jump size 4 lands on 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 and 24, the treasure opens, and 4 goes into the list. Jump size 5 lands on 20 and then 25, and a small arc over 24 shows Jumpy hopping over the treasure. The student tries more sizes until the list holds 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 24, including 1 and 24 themselves. The solved card pairs them as 1 and 24, 2 and 12, 3 and 8, 4 and 6, and names these numbers the factors of 24, the numbers that divide it exactly.

Then the student sets two treasures and looks for sizes that reach both. On 14 and 36 a jump of 7 lands on 14, then 21, 28, 35 and 42, and the path shows that it jumps over 36. The list soon shows that 1 and 2 reach both, and these are called the common factors. The remaining cards are treasures on 15 and 30 (1, 3, 5, 15), on 28 and 70 (1, 2, 7, 14), on 20 and 28 (1, 2, 4), and on 12 and 18, where the student names the biggest size that reaches both (6). If the student lists a size that does not work for both, the tool replays it and shows the path landing on one treasure and jumping over the other. A size the student leaves out, such as 1 or the treasure number itself, is pointed out on the line with its landing spots.

Hints come in order: where does Jumpy land with this jump size; a jump size works if it divides the treasure number exactly, so check 1 and the number itself too; try each jump size from 1 upward and mark the ones that land on the treasure; and last the working sizes are shown on the line and a similar card follows. Through doing, the student learns that the factors of a number are the jump sizes that land exactly on it, that 1 and the number are always among them, that common factors are the sizes that reach two numbers, and that the landing spots are multiples while the jump size is a factor.

topics.summary: A factor divides a number exactly; the jump sizes that reach a number are its factors, and those that reach two numbers are their common factors.

content.text:
Jumpy and Grumpy play a game.
Grumpy places a treasure on some number. For example, he may place it on 24.
Jumpy chooses a jump size. If he chooses 4, then he has to jump only on multiples of 4, starting at 0.
Jumpy gets the treasure if he lands on the number where Grumpy placed it.
Which jump sizes will get Jumpy to land on 24?
If he chooses 4: Jumpy lands on 4 → 8 → 12 → 16 → 20 → 24 → 28 → … Other successful jump sizes are 2, 3, 6, 8 and 12.
What about the jump of sizes 1 and 24? Yes, they also will land on 24.
The numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24 all divide 24 exactly. Recall that such numbers are called factors or divisors of 24.

content.text:
Grumpy increases the level of the game. Two treasures are kept on two different numbers. Jumpy has to choose a jump size and stick to it. Jumpy gets the treasures only if he lands on both the numbers with the chosen jump size. As before, Jumpy starts at 0.
Grumpy has kept the treasures on 14 and 36. And, Jumpy chooses a jump size of 7.
Will Jumpy land on both the treasures? Starting from 0, he jumps to 7 → 14 → 21 → 28 → 35 → 42 … We see that he landed on 14 but did not land on 36, so he does not get the treasure. What jump size should he have chosen?
The factors of 14 are: 1, 2, 7, 14. So, these jump sizes will land on 14.
The factors of 36 are: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18 and 36. These jump sizes will land on 36.
So, the jump sizes of 1 or 2 will land on both 14 and 36. Notice that 1 and 2 are the common factors of 14 and 36.
The jump sizes using which both the treasures can be reached are the common factors of the two numbers where the treasures are placed.
What jump size can reach both 15 and 30? There are multiple jump sizes possible. Try to find them all.

A factor of a number divides it exactly, and 1 and the number itself are always factors.
A common factor of two numbers is a factor of both.
A multiple is bigger than or equal to the number; a factor is smaller than or equal to it.

narration: Kiko has one question to ask.
What is the real-life use case?
A shopkeeper has two ropes, fifteen metres long and thirty metres long.
He cuts both into equal pieces with no rope left over.
A piece of five metres works, because five is a common factor of fifteen and thirty.

narration: Kiko has one question to ask.
What mistake do some students make here?
Some students say only three and five work, and one and fifteen are not real jump values.
But a jump of one reaches every number, thirty included.
A jump of fifteen reaches fifteen and then thirty, so both are real jump values.

media.instructions_for_student: A number is arranged in rows and columns of dots; the number of ways is the number of factor pairs, and a prime has only one way.
media.description:
A tray of loose dot counters sits on the left of the screen, with a stepper that sets how many dots it holds, from 1 to 60, and a Make Rectangles button beneath it. The wide area on the right is empty, ready to hold boxes of figs drawn as rows and columns of dots.

On each card the student first guesses how many different rectangles the dots can make, then sets the number and presses the button. The tool lays out every rectangle, each labelled with its rows and columns. For 12 dots it draws 1 by 12, 2 by 6 and 3 by 4, and a small turn-round mark shows that 6 by 2 is the same box turned on its side. A count underneath lists the factors, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12, and says there are six. For 7 dots only one rectangle appears, 1 by 7, and the only factors are 1 and 7. The student sees that the rows times the columns always give the number, so both are factors. Then the student types the factors or taps a coloured tag: prime, composite or neither.

The six cards are: 12 dots, list all the factors; 7 dots, how many rectangles (one, so 7 is prime); 18 dots, how many factors (six, from 1 by 18, 2 by 9 and 3 by 6); 1 dot, prime, composite or neither (neither: a single box with one factor, while a prime needs exactly two); find an even number below 30 with exactly two factors (only 2, because 4, 6, 8 and the rest each make more than one rectangle); and find all the primes from 21 to 30 (23 and 29, while 25 makes 1 by 25 and 5 by 5 and so has three factors).

A wrong tag shows the count of factors beside the rule, exactly two factors means prime and more than two means composite. A missed factor pair shows as a missing rectangle, and a solved card shows the rectangles and the factor count together. Hints come in order: how many rows and how many columns can the dots make; each pair of rows and columns multiplies to the number, so both are factors; try rows 1, 2, 3 and so on in turn and stop when the columns become smaller than the rows; and last the rectangles are shown with their factors and a similar card follows. Through doing, the student learns that each rectangle is a pair of factors, that a prime makes only one rectangle, that 2 is an even prime, and that 1 is neither prime nor composite.

narration: Kiko has one question to ask.
What is the real-life use case?
A school hall has chairs in four rows of six.
Four times six is twenty four, because every row has six chairs.
So the rows and the chairs in a row are factors of twenty four.

narration: Kiko has one question to ask.
What mistake do some students make here?
Some students say rows plus columns make twelve.
Take two rows of six figs, and two plus six is only eight.
Two times six is twelve, so we multiply, because adding does not count the figs.

content.text:
Guna and Anshu want to pack figs (anjeer) that grow in their farm. Guna wants to put 12 figs in each box and Anshu wants to put 7 figs in each box.
How many arrangements are possible?
Think and find out the different ways how, 1. Guna can arrange 12 figs in a rectangular manner. 2. Anshu can arrange 7 figs in a rectangular manner.
Guna has listed out these possibilities.
Observe the number of rows and columns in each of the arrangements. How are they related to 12?

content.text:
Numbers that have only two factors are called prime numbers or primes. Here are the first few primes, 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19. Notice that the factors of a prime number are 1 and the number itself.
What about numbers that have more than two factors? They are called composite numbers. The first few composite numbers are, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 20.
What about 1, which has only one factor? The number 1 is neither a prime nor a composite number.
How many prime numbers are there from 21 to 30? How many composite numbers are there from 21 to 30?

2. 1 has only one factor, itself. A prime needs exactly two factors, so 1 is not prime.
3. Numbers with exactly two factors, like 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, are primes.
4. Numbers with more than two factors, like 4, 6, 8, 9, are composite.

A number with more than two factors is composite.
1 has one factor and is neither prime nor composite.

steps: a) There is no prime number whose units digit is 4.: True; units digit 4 means even, and 2 is the only even prime.
b) A product of primes can also be prime.: False; a product of primes is composite.
c) Prime numbers do not have any factors.: False; a prime has exactly two factors, 1 and itself.
d) All even numbers are composite numbers.: False; all even numbers except 2 are composite.

e) 2 is a prime and so is the next number, 3. For every other prime, the next number is composite.: True; every other pair of consecutive numbers contains an even number greater than 2, which is composite.

media.description:
A 10 by 10 board holding the numbers 1 to 100 fills the screen. Below it are a Next step button and a counter that reads Primes found: 0. All the numbers start plain.

Before each press the student predicts by tapping the number that the sieve will circle next. Then the student presses Next step and watches. The first press crosses out 1, because it is neither prime nor composite. The next press circles 2 in green and flashes each of its multiples, 4, 6, 8 and on, as it turns them grey. The press after that circles 3, the first number still uncrossed, and flashes 6, 9, 12 and the rest. The following presses circle 5 and then 7. The counter rises with each circle, and the student keeps pressing until every number is either circled or crossed out. Circling 11 crosses nothing new, because all its multiples up to 100 are already grey, and the remaining uncrossed numbers are circled one after another.

The student can also tap any number and say prime or composite. A tap on a crossed-out number shows the circled number that removed it: 91 shows that 7 crossed it out as 7 times 13, so a crossed number is a multiple of a smaller circled number and has a third factor. A number left uncrossed has no smaller circled number dividing it, so it has only two factors. Numbers such as 9, 15, 25 and 49 are odd and stay open after the step for 2, yet later steps remove them, so odd does not mean prime. When the board is finished, the long grey stretch from 90 to 96, between the primes 89 and 97, shows how many composite numbers can sit in a row.

The six cards are: after circling 2 and 3, which number is circled next (5, since 4 is already crossed out); how many primes there are from 1 to 30 (10); how many from 1 to 100 (25); the number that 7 crosses out which 2, 3 and 5 did not (49, which is 7 times 7; the same step also removes 77 and 91 for the first time, and the tool shows all three, the card asks for the smallest); all the twin primes up to 30 (3 and 5, 5 and 7, 11 and 13, 17 and 19); and the largest prime below 100 (97). Hints come in order: which number is the first one left uncrossed; the first uncrossed number is prime, so cross out its multiples; circle it, cross out its multiples and look for the next uncrossed number; and last the tool does the next step and shows why the number is prime, and a similar card follows. Through doing, the student learns that the sieve is not magic: what survives every crossing has no factor except 1 and itself.

content.text:
Can we list all the prime numbers from 1 to 100?
Here is an interesting way to find prime numbers. Just follow the steps given below and see what happens.
Step 1: Cross out 1 because it is neither prime nor composite.
Step 2: Circle 2, and then cross out all multiples of 2 after that, i.e., 4, 6, 8, and so on.
Step 3: You will find that the next uncrossed number is 3. Circle 3 and then cross out all the multiples of 3 after that, i.e., 6, 9, 12, and so on.
Step 4: The next uncrossed number is 5. Circle 5 and then cross out all the multiples of 5 after that, i.e., 10, 15, 20, and so on.
Step 5: Continue this process till all the numbers in the list are either circled or crossed out.
All the circled numbers are prime numbers. All the crossed out numbers, other than 1, are composite numbers. This method is called the Sieve of Eratosthenes.
This procedure can be carried on for numbers greater than 100 also. Eratosthenes was a Greek mathematician who lived around 2200 years ago and developed this method of listing primes.

Answer: Circled numbers have exactly two factors, so they are prime; crossed-out numbers have more, so they are composite.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about prime pairs.
<bookmark mark='cards'/>Take the prime numbers below twenty and pair them up.

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Two and three, three and seven, and two and thirteen are the three pairs.

media.instructions_for_student: A thread tied to every gap-th peg of a circle reaches every peg exactly when the number of pegs and the gap are co-prime.
media.description:
A circle of pegs, like a thread-art board, opens with 12 pegs numbered 0 to 11 round the edge. Two steppers sit beside it, one for the number of pegs from 6 to 24 and one for the thread gap from 1 to 12, with a Draw button and a read-out that shows the pegs reached and a co-prime tick.

On each card the student first predicts whether the thread will touch every peg. Then the student sets the pegs and the gap and presses Draw. The thread is tied to peg 0 and then drawn one segment at a time to every gap-th peg, and each peg it touches turns gold. It stops when it comes back to the start, and the pegs it missed stay grey. With 12 pegs and gap 4 the thread touches only 0, 4 and 8, and the nine grey pegs show that 12 and 4 share the common factor 4, so the tick stays off. With 13 pegs and gap 4 the thread reaches all 13 pegs and the tick comes on, although 4 is not a prime. With 12 pegs and gap 5 every peg is gold. With 10 pegs and gap 4 the thread touches 0, 4, 8, 2 and 6, five pegs, the even ones, because 10 and 4 share the factor 2.

The six cards are: 12 pegs, gap 4, does the thread reach every peg (no, 12 and 4 share 4); 13 pegs, gap 4 (yes, 13 and 4 are co-prime); 12 pegs, gap 5 (every peg); find a gap below 12 for 12 pegs that reaches every peg (5, 7 or 11, and gap 1 works trivially); 10 pegs, gap 4, how many pegs are reached (5); and which of 18 and 35, 15 and 37, 30 and 415 are co-prime (18 and 35, and 15 and 37). The numbers on the last card are too big for the board, so the pegs are replaced by two factor lists that the student fills in for each pair, and 30 and 415 are caught by the common factor 5.

A wrong co-prime answer shows the common factor of the two numbers, and a solved card shows the pegs reached with the tick. Hints come in order: which pegs does the thread touch; the thread reaches every peg when the two numbers have no common factor other than 1; list the factors of both numbers and look for one besides 1; and last the common factor is shown with the pegs it misses, and a similar card follows. Through doing, the student learns that two numbers are co-prime when their only common factor is 1, that a thread with gap g on n pegs reaches every peg exactly when n and g are co-prime, and that co-prime numbers need not be prime.

content.text:
Let us go back to the treasure finding game. This time, treasures are kept on two numbers. Jumpy gets the treasures only if he is able to reach both the numbers with the same jump size. There is also a new rule, a jump size of 1 is not allowed.
Where should Grumpy place the treasures so that Jumpy cannot reach both the treasures?
Will placing the treasure on 12 and 26 work? No! If the jump size is chosen to be 2, then Jumpy will reach both 12 and 26.
What about 4 and 9? Jumpy cannot reach both using any jump size other than 1. So, Grumpy knows that the pair 4 and 9 is safe.
What is special about safe pairs? They don’t have any common factor other than 1. Two numbers are said to be co-prime to each other if they have no common factor other than 1.
Example: As 15 and 39 have 3 as a common factor, they are not co-prime. But 4 and 9 are co-prime.

content.text:
1. Predict first: the first common multiple of 3 and 5 is 15. How does it compare with 3 × 5?
2. 3 × 5 = 15, the same. For 4 and 9 the first common multiple is 36, which is 4 × 9.
3. For 3 and 6 the first common multiple is 6, less than 3 × 6 = 18.
4. When the pair is co-prime, the first common multiple is the product.

media.instructions_for_student: Breaking a number into two factors again and again ends in the same primes whichever way it is split.
media.description:
The student opens a blank canvas with the number 72 at the top of a tree. A Split button sits below it, and a bar along the bottom reads Primes found, empty at the start. Prime leaves will turn green and composite leaves will stay open, so the student can always see what is still to be broken down.

The student taps the number or any open leaf, presses Split, and types two numbers that multiply to it, for example 12 and 6 for 72. If they do not multiply to the number the split is turned back with the product shown, such as 8 times 6 is 48, not 72. A split into 1 and the number itself is also turned back, since it gets nowhere. Each correct split grows two branches. A leaf that is prime turns green and drops into the bar in increasing order, while a composite leaf stays open and shows its factors waiting, for example 4 shows 2 and 2 still to come. The student splits 12 into 3 and 4, 4 into 2 and 2, and 6 into 2 and 3, and the bar ends as 2, 2, 2, 3, 3. The primes of 12 and of 6 are seen joining in the bar, so the primes of 72 are the primes of its two factors put together. Multiplying the bar back gives 72.

The six cards are: 72, build a tree and write its prime factorisation (2 times 2 times 2 times 3 times 3); 72 again with a different tree, such as 8 times 9 or 2 times 36, and compare the leaves (same primes, so the solved card puts the two trees side by side); 64 (six 2s); 105 (3 times 5 times 7); a number with one 2, two 3s and one 11, where the student multiplies prime tiles to get 198 and checks by splitting it; and three primes below 30 whose product is 1955, where the student starts from 1955, tries primes from the tray, and finds 5, 17 and 23.

Hints come in order: which two numbers multiply to the number on this leaf; split every composite leaf and stop only when every leaf is prime; start with the smallest prime that divides the number; and last the tree is finished and the primes are read out in order, and a similar card follows. Through doing, the student learns that a number is broken down until only primes are left, that different trees of one number end in the same primes, and that the order of multiplying makes no difference.

media.description: Thirty six is broken into primes in four ways, starting from two times eighteen, three times twelve, four times nine and six times six. Each way ends with two twos and two threes, and multiplying back gives thirty six every time. Keeko doubts this and says different starts must give different primes.

video_script.why: The child sees that four different ways of breaking thirty six all end with two twos and two threes, and that multiplying back gives thirty six.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the number thirty six.
<bookmark mark='ways'/>It is broken in four ways.
The ways start with two times eighteen, three times twelve, four times nine and six times six.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Each way is broken until only primes are left.
Do the four ways end the same?

narration: <bookmark mark='first'/>Step one, break the first two ways.
Two times eighteen breaks into two times two times nine, and then into two, two, three, three.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Three times twelve breaks into three times three times four, and then into three, three, two, two.
We keep breaking, because a factor that is not prime can break again.

marks.third: the third tree breaks 4 into 2 × 2 and 9 into 3 × 3
marks.fourth: the fourth tree breaks each 6 into 2 × 3

narration: <bookmark mark='third'/>Step two, break the last two ways.
Four times nine breaks into two, two, three, three.
<bookmark mark='fourth'/>Six times six breaks each six into two times three, which gives two, three, two, three.
Six is not a prime, so each six breaks into two times three.

narration: <bookmark mark='count'/>Step three, count the primes in each way.

narration: <bookmark mark='twos'/>Step four, multiply back to check.
Two times two is four.
<bookmark mark='threes'/>Three times three is nine.
<bookmark mark='join'/>Four times nine is thirty six, and order does not change this.
The check works, because multiplying is the opposite of breaking.
beats.on_screen: Step 4: check by multiplying back: 2 × 2 = 4 and 3 × 3 = 9, then 4 × 9 = 36

marks.ans: the answer is boxed in green

content.text:
Teacher: Are 56 and 63 co-prime?
Anshu and Guna: If they have a common factor other than 1, then they are not co-prime. Let us check.
Anshu: I can write 56 = 14 × 4 and 63 = 21 × 3. So, 14 and 4 are factors, of 56. Further, 21 and 3 are factors of 63. So, there are no common factors. The numbers are co-prime.
Guna: Hold on. I can also write 56 = 7 × 8 and 63 = 9 × 7. We see that 7 is a factor of both numbers, so, they are not co-prime.
Clearly Guna is right, as 7 is a common factor.
But where did Anshu go wrong?
Writing 56 = 14 × 4 tells us that 14 and 4 are both factors of 56, but it does not tell all the factors of 56. The same holds for the factors of 63.
Try another example: 80 and 63. There are many ways to factorise both numbers.
80 = 40 × 2 = 20 × 4 = 10 × 8 = 16 × 5 = ???
63 = 9 × 7 = 3 × 21 = ???
We have written '???' to say that there may be more ways to factorise these numbers. But if we take any of the given factorisations, for example, 80 = 16 × 5 and 63 = 9 × 7, then there are no common factors. Can we conclude that 80 and 63 are co-prime? As Anshu's mistake above shows, we cannot conclude that as there may be other ways to factorise the numbers.
What this means is that we need a more systematic approach to check if two numbers are co-prime.

content.text:
Take a number such as 56. It is composite, as we saw that it can be written as 56 = 4 × 14. So, both 4 and 14 are factors of 56. Now take one of these, say 14. It is also composite and can be written as 14 = 2 × 7. Therefore, 56 = 4 × 2 × 7. Now, 4 is composite and can be written as 4 = 2 × 2. Therefore, 56 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 7. All the factors appearing here, 2 and 7, are prime numbers. So, we cannot divide them further.
In conclusion, we have written 56 as a product of prime numbers. This is called prime factorisation of 56. The individual factors are called prime factors. For example, the prime factors of 56 are 2 and 7.
Every number greater than 1 has a prime factorisation. The idea is the same: keep breaking the composite numbers into factors till only primes are left.
The number 1 does not have any prime factorisation. It is not divisible by any prime number.
What is the prime factorisation of a prime number like 7? It is just 7 (we cannot break it down any further).
Let us see a few more examples.
By going through different ways of breaking down the number, we wrote 63 as 3 × 3 × 7 and as 3 × 7 × 3. Are they different? Not really! The same prime numbers 3 and 7 occur in both cases. Further, 3 appears two times in both and 7 appears once.
Here, you see four different ways to get prime factorisation of 36. Observe that in all four cases, we get two 2s and two 3s.
Multiply back to see that you get 36 in all four cases.
For any number, it is a remarkable fact that there is only one prime factorisation, except that the prime factors may come in different orders. As we explain below, the order is not important. However, as we saw in these examples, there are many ways to arrive at the prime factorisation!
Using this diagram, can you explain why 30 = 2 × 3 × 5, no matter which way you multiply 2, 3, and 5?
When multiplying numbers, we can do so in any order. The end result is the same. That is why, when two 2s and two 3s are multiplied in any order, we get 36. In a later class, we shall study this under the names of commutativity and associativity of multiplication.
Thus, the order does not matter. Usually we write the prime numbers in increasing order. For example, 225 = 3 × 3 × 5 × 5 or 30 = 2 × 3 × 5.

Worked example: Using this diagram, can you explain why 30 = 2 × 3 × 5, no matter which way you multiply 2, 3, and 5?
1. The diagram is a cuboid made of unit cubes with 3 cubes along the front width, 2 along the height and 5 along the depth, so it has 2 × 3 × 5 = 30 cubes. Counting the same cubes layer by layer in any direction gives the same total, so the order of multiplication does not change the product. (Commutativity and associativity of multiplication, to be studied in a later class.)

When we find the prime factorisation of a number, we first write it as a product of two factors. For example, 72 = 12 × 6. Then, we find the prime factorisation of each of the factors. In the above example, 12 = 2 × 2 × 3 and 6 = 2 × 3. Now, can you say what the prime factorisation of 72 is?
The prime factorisation of the original number is obtained by putting these together.
72 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 2 × 3
We can also write this as 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. Multiply and check that you get 72 back!
Observe how many times each prime factor occurs in the factorisation of 72.
Compare it with how many times it occurs in the factorisations of 12 and 6 put together.

media.instructions_for_student: Writing two numbers as products of primes shows at once whether they share a prime factor, and whether the primes of one are all inside the other.
media.description:
Two number boxes sit side by side at the top of the screen. Under each one the prime factorisation appears as a row of coloured tiles, one colour for each prime, in increasing order, with the two rows lined up one above the other. Between them is a shared-primes marker, and below are two verdicts to fill in: co-prime, yes or no, and divisible, yes or no.

The student types two numbers, for example 56 and 63, and predicts both verdicts before touching the tiles. The rows show 56 as 2, 2, 2, 7 and 63 as 3, 3, 7. The student then matches tiles by dragging each tile of the smaller number onto an unused tile of the same colour in the bigger number's row. Tiles of the same colour in both rows light up in the shared marker, so the 7 in both is seen at once and the pair is not co-prime. For divisibility every tile of the smaller number needs its own partner. Tiles that find no match turn red, so the student sees which primes are missing.

The six cards are: 56 and 63, co-prime (no, they share 7); 40 and 231, co-prime (yes, 2 and 5 against 3, 7 and 11); 168 and 12, is 168 divisible by 12 (yes, 2, 2, 3 find partners and the 2 and 7 left over make 14); 75 and 21, is 75 divisible by 21 (no, the 7 of 21 has no partner in 3, 5, 5); 42 and 12, is 42 divisible by 12 (no, 12 needs two 2s and 42 has only one, even though every prime colour of 12 appears in 42); and 30 and 45, where both answers are no, because they share 3 and 5 and the 2 of 30 has no partner in 45.

A wrong verdict shows the shared tiles highlighted, or the red tiles for divisibility, and a solved card shows both verdicts with the tiles. Hints come in order: what colours do the two rows share; no shared prime means co-prime and every prime of the smaller inside the bigger means divisible; count each prime in both rows and compare the counts; and last the tiles are matched and the verdicts read out, and a similar card follows. Through doing, the student learns that no common prime means the numbers are co-prime, that one number divides another when its primes, count by count, sit inside the other's, and that a shared prime alone is not enough for division.

content.text:
Let us again take the numbers 56 and 63. How can we check if they are co-prime? We can use the prime factorisation of both numbers, 
56 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 7 and 63 = 3 × 3 × 7
Now, we see that 7 is a prime factor of 56 as well as 63. Therefore, 56 and 63 are not co-prime.
What about 80 and 63? Their prime factorisations are as follows:
80 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 5 and 63 = 3 × 3 × 7
There are no common prime factors. Can we conclude that they are co-prime? Suppose they have a common factor that is composite. Would the prime factors of this composite common factor appear in the prime factorisation of 80 and 63?
Therefore, we can say that if there are no common prime factors, then the two numbers are co-prime.
Let us see some examples.
Example: Consider 40 and 231. Their prime factorisations are as follows: 40 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 5 and 231 = 3 × 7 × 11
We see that there are no common primes that divide both 40 and 231. Indeed, the prime factors of 40 are 2 and 5 while, the prime factors of 231 are 3, 7, and 11. Therefore, 40 and 231 are co-prime!
Example: Consider 242 and 195. Their prime factorisations are as follows: 242 = 2 × 11 × 11 and 195 = 3 × 5 × 13
The prime factors of 242 are 2 and 11. The prime factors of 195 are 3, 5, and 13. There are no common prime factors. Therefore, 242 and 195 are co-prime.

content.text:
We can say that if one number is divisible by another, the prime factorisation of the second number is included in the prime factorisation of the first number.
We say that 48 is divisible by 12 because when we divide 48 by 12, the remainder is zero. How can we check if one number is divisible by another without carrying out long division?
Example: Is 168 divisible by 12? Find the prime factorisations of both: 168 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 and 12 = 2 × 2 × 3
Since we can multiply in any order, now it is clear that, 168 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 2 × 7 = 12 × 14
Therefore, 168 is divisible by 12.
Example: Is 75 divisible by 21? Find the prime factorisations of both: 75 = 3 × 5 × 5 and 21 = 3 × 7
As we saw in the discussion above, if 75 was a multiple of 21, then all prime factors of 21 would also be prime factors of 75. However, 7 is a prime factor of 21 but not a prime factor of 75. Therefore, 75 is not divisible by 21.
Example: Is 42 divisible by 12? Find the prime factorisations of both: 42 = 2 × 3 × 7 and 12 = 2 × 2 × 3
All prime factors of 12 are also prime factors of 42. But the prime factorisation of 12 is not included in the prime factorisation of 42. This is because 2 occurs twice in the prime factorisation of 12 but only once in the prime factorisation of 42. This means that 42 is not divisible by 12.
We can say that if one number is divisible by another, then the prime factorisation of the second number is included in the prime factorisation of the first number.

media.description:
A large number box sits at the top of the screen, and a round glass lens covers only its last digit while the other digits are dimmed. Below it are three test lights labelled for 10, for 5 and for 2, all off at the start, and a Check by division button.

The student types a number, reads only what the lens shows and switches on the lights they think are right. The lens also names the rule for each light in a word. Pressing Check by division makes the tool divide by 10, 5 and 2, and the remainders appear beside each light so the student sees whether the prediction matched. For 8560 the lens shows 0 and all three lights come on, with remainders 0, 0 and 0. For 125 the lens shows 5, only the light for 5 comes on, and the remainders are 5, 0 and 1. For 682 the lens shows 2, only the light for 2 comes on, and the remainders are 2, 2 and 0. For 173 the lens shows 3, no light comes on, and the remainders are 3, 3 and 1.

The six cards are: 8560, which of 10, 5 and 2 divide it (all three); 125 (5 only); 682 (2 only); 173 (none); find the largest number below 399 divisible by 5, where the student tries 398, 397, 396 and sees the last digit fall to 5 (395); and the remainders of 2345 on dividing by 10, 5 and 2 (5, 0 and 1), which the student reads from the last digit 5 and then confirms with the division.

A wrong prediction shows the remainder from the division. This also corrects the idea that only numbers ending in 5 are multiples of 5, since 8560 and 20 end in 0 and still light the 5 light. A solved card shows the last digit and the three lights. Hints come in order: which digit does the lens show; the last digit alone decides 10, 5 and 2; check whether it is 0, whether it is 0 or 5, and whether it is even; and last the lights are lit and the remainders shown, and a similar card follows. Through doing, the student learns that a number is divisible by 10 when it ends in 0, by 5 when it ends in 0 or 5, and by 2 when it ends in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8, without any long division.

content.text:
So far, we have been finding factors of numbers in different contexts, including to determine if a number is prime or not, or if a given pair of numbers is co-prime or not.
It is easy to find factors of small numbers. How do we find factors of a large number?
Let us take 8560. Does it have any factors from 2 to 10 (2, 3, 4, 5, ..., 9, 10)?
It is easy to check if some of these numbers are factors or not without doing long division. Can you find them?
Let us take 10. Is 8560 divisible by 10? This is another way of asking if 10 is a factor of 8560.
For this, we can look at the pattern in the multiples of 10.
The first few multiples of 10 are: 10, 20, 30, 40, ... Continue this sequence and observe the pattern.
Is 125 a multiple of 10? Will this number appear in the previous sequence? Why or why not?
Can you now answer if 8560 is divisible by 10?
Math Talk: Consider this statement: Numbers that are divisible by 10 are those that end with '0'. Do you agree?

content.text:
Worked example: Let us take 8560. Does it have any factors from 2 to 10 (2, 3, 4, 5, ..., 9, 10)? It is easy to check if some of these numbers are factors or not without doing long division. Can you find them?
1. 10 divides 8560 because it ends in 0; 5 and 2 divide it for the same reason.
2. 4 and 8 divide it too: 60 is a multiple of 4 and 560 is a multiple of 8.
3. 3, 6, 7 and 9 do not divide 8560 exactly.
Answer: 2, 4, 5, 8 and 10.

media.instructions_for_student: Divisibility by 4 depends on the last two digits and divisibility by 8 on the last three.
media.description:
A number box holding 8536 sits above a lens window that starts over the last two digits and can be widened to three. Two test lights, for 4 and for 8, are off at the start. Beside the number is a Check by division button and a short list of the multiples of 4 and of 8 that lie near the number inside the lens window.

The student types a number, slides the lens to two digits or three, reads the number in the window and predicts the lights before pressing Check by division. For 8536 the window reads 36, the list shows 32, 36 and 40, and the student sees that 36 is a multiple of 4, so the 4 light comes on. A note shows why the digits outside the lens cannot change the answer: they stand for hundreds, and 100 is a multiple of 4. For 8, the 8 light stays dim while the lens is two digits wide. If the student tries it anyway, the tool shows 108 and 208, both ending in 08, and the list shows that 208 is a multiple of 8 and 108 is not, since 104 and 112 come either side of it. Widening the lens to three digits settles it, because 1000 is a multiple of 8.

The six cards are: 8536, is it divisible by 4 (yes, 36 is); 1732 and 1736, which is divisible by 4 (both, 32 and 36); 8560, change the last two digits to make a multiple of 8 (8552, since 552 is 8 times 69; 8560 itself already works because 560 is 8 times 70, and the card asks for a changed number); 1128, is it divisible by 8 (yes, 128 is); the largest 4-digit palindrome divisible by 4, where the student finds that 9 at both ends gives an odd number and 8998 fails because 98 is not on the list (8888); and 2024 to 2099, how many leap years (19, from 2024 to 2096 in steps of 4).

A wrong prediction shows why, with the digits beyond the lens as multiples of 100 or 1000. A solved card shows the digits used and the light. Hints come in order: how many digits does the lens show; for 4 look at the last two digits and for 8 look at the last three; divide only the number in the lens by 4 or by 8; and last the lens number and the answer are shown, and a similar card follows. Through doing, the student learns that the last digit cannot decide 4, since 12 and 22 differ, that the last two digits decide 4, and that the last three digits decide 8.

100 = 25 x 4 and 1000 = 250 x 4, so hundreds and thousands are whole fours
the last two digits in every range are 32 and 36; 32 = 4 x 8 and 36 = 4 x 9
so a number is a multiple of 4 when its last two digits make a multiple of 4

content.text:
Checking if a number is divisible by 4 can also be done easily!
Look at its multiples: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, ...
Are you able to observe any patterns that can be used? The multiples of 10, 5 and 2 have a pattern in their last digits which we are able to use to check for divisibility. Similarly, can we check if a number is divisible by 4 by looking at the last digit?
It does not work! Look at 12 and 22. They have the same last digit, but 12 is a multiple of 4 while 22 is not. Similarly 14 and 24 have the same last digit, but 14 is not a multiple of 4 while 24 is. Similarly, 16 and 26 or 18 and 28. What this means is that by looking at the last digit, we cannot tell whether a number is a multiple of 4.

4. So the last digit alone cannot test divisibility by 4.

content.text:
Is 8536 divisible by 4?
Consider these statements: 1. Only the last two digits matter when deciding if a given number is divisible by 4. 2. If the number formed by the last two digits is divisible by 4, then the original number is divisible by 4. 3. If the original number is divisible by 4, then the number formed by the last two digits is divisible by 4. Do you agree? Why or why not?

maths_rules: 100 = 25 x 4 and 1000 = 250 x 4, so the hundreds part of any number is a whole number of fours
so the hundreds part never changes the answer, and only the last two digits matter
124 = 100 + 24, with 100 = 25 fours and 24 = 6 fours, so 124 = 31 fours
364 = 300 + 64, with 300 = 75 fours and 64 = 16 fours, so 364 = 91 fours
if the whole and the hundreds part are whole fours, then so is the difference, which is the last two digits
1200 = 12 hundreds = 12 x 25 fours = 300 fours, and 00 = 0 = 0 x 4

content.question_tex: Find the largest and smallest $4$-digit numbers that are divisible by $4$ and are also palindromes.

steps: The first and last digits are equal, so the last digit is even for divisibility by 4: the number starts with 2, 4, 6 or 8.
Largest: 8 b b 8 with b as big as possible and the last two digits a multiple of 4. 88 is a multiple of 4, but 98 is not, so b = 8: 8888.
Smallest: 2 b b 2 with b as small as possible. 02 is not a multiple of 4, but 12 is, so b = 1: 2112.
content.answer: Largest 8888, smallest 2112 (the printed answers 9999 and 1001 are odd numbers).

content.answer_tex: Largest $8888$, smallest $2112$ (the printed answers $9999$ and $1001$ are odd numbers).

content.text:
Worked example: Interestingly, even checking for divisibility by 8 can be simplified. Can the last two digits be used for this?
1. 108 and 208 end in the same two digits, 08.
2. 208 = 8 × 26, so 208 is divisible by 8; 108 is between 104 = 8 × 13 and 112 = 8 × 14, so 108 is not.
3. So the last two digits cannot decide divisibility by 8. 1000 = 8 × 125 is a multiple of 8, so three digits are needed.
Answer: No: the last two digits are not enough for 8; the last three digits are needed.

2. The last three digits are 560 = 8 × 70, which is already a multiple of 8, so 8560 itself works.
3. Keeping the hundreds digit 5, 552 = 8 × 69 also works, so 8552 is a multiple of 8.
4. Only the last three digits matter, and the rule works both ways.

8 covers 4 and 2, and 10 needs 2 and 5.
5 and 8 together cover all of 2, 4, 5, 8 and 10.
Factors of 10000 are only 2s and 5s, so a pair with no zero ending uses all the 2s in one number and all the 5s in the other.

content.question: Write two numbers whose product is 10000. The two numbers should not have 0 as the units digit.
content.text: Write two numbers whose product is $10000$. The two numbers should not have $0$ as the units digit.
content.publication_text: Write two numbers whose product is $10000$. The two numbers should not have $0$ as the units digit.
content.question_tex: Write two numbers whose product is $10000$. The two numbers should not have $0$ as the units digit.

steps: 10000 is four 2s and four 5s multiplied together.
Put all the 2s in one number and all the 5s in the other: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 is 16 and 5 × 5 × 5 × 5 is 625.
Neither 16 nor 625 ends in 0, and 16 × 625 = 10000.
content.question: Write two numbers whose product is 10000. The two numbers should not have 0 as the units digit.
content.text:
$1$. $10000$ is four $2s$ and four $5s$ multiplied together.
$2$. Put all the $2s$ in one number and all the $5s$ in the other: $2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2$ is $16$ and $5 \times 5 \times 5 \times 5$ is $625$.
$3$. Neither $16$ nor $625$ ends in $0$, and $16 \times 625 = 10000$.
Answer: $16 \times 625 = 10000$

media.instructions_for_student: A grid of primes is filled so that each row and each column multiplies to the number beside it, using prime factorisation of the clue.
media.description:
A 3 by 3 grid of empty cells fills the middle of the screen. The row products are written to the right of the rows and the column products below the columns, and a read-out under each line shows the product of what is placed in it. Under the grid is a prime keypad with 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17 and 19. Tiles from the keypad drop into cells, and a number can also be typed into a cell.

The first four cards open only one line of the grid at a time. On a row of 30 the student breaks the clue into primes and drops 2, 3 and 5 into the three cells in any order, and the read-out turns green at 30. The student can swap the order and see it still gives 30. A row of 27 takes 3, 3 and 3, a row of 8 takes 2, 2 and 2, and a column of 105 takes 3, 5 and 7. A tile that is not prime, such as 15 or 6, is refused and the keypad reminds that only primes are allowed.

On the fifth card the whole grid opens with every clue given, for example row products 105, 20 and 30 and column products 28, 125 and 18. The student writes each clue as primes first: 105 is 3, 5, 7; 20 is 2, 2, 5; 30 is 2, 3, 5; 28 is 2, 2, 7; 125 is 5, 5, 5; 18 is 2, 3, 3. Starting with the clue that has the fewest choices, 125 can only be 5 times 5 times 5, so the middle column is all 5s, and the 7 in 28 can only come from the first row, which fixes the rest. The finished grid reads 7, 5, 3 then 2, 5, 2 then 2, 5, 3. On the sixth card the student fills a second puzzle, with row products 8, 105 and 70 and column products 30, 70 and 28, and checks it by multiplying every row and column by hand and typing the six products before the read-outs are shown.

A product that does not match is shown beside its clue, and a solved puzzle shows every row and column product. Hints come in order: which primes multiply to the clue; break the clue into primes, since each cell holds one prime of its row and column; start with the clue that has the fewest prime factors; and last the row is filled and the column products are checked, and a similar puzzle follows. Through doing, the student learns that every clue breaks into primes in only one way apart from order, and that this single breakdown, checked against rows and columns together, solves the puzzle.

video_script.anchor: an empty 3 by 3 grid with 105, 20 and 30 at the right of the rows and 28, 125 and 18 below the columns
video_script.design: One idea: begin with the product that has only one choice and let each filled cell fix the next. Assumes the rules of the puzzle and prime factors. Wrong idea: a composite number can sit in a cell. The grid stays on the board to the end.
source: Fill the 3 by 3 grid with prime numbers only so that the product of each row is the number to the right of the row and the product of each column is the number below the column. Row products: 105, 20, 30. Column products: 28, 125, 18.
never_show: the second row can have a four in it
video_script.wrong_move: Kiko says the second row can have a four in it, because four times five is twenty. Four is two times two, so it is not a prime, and the bubble is struck through.
maths_rules: 125 = 5 x 5 x 5, so the middle column is 5, 5, 5
105 = 3 x 5 x 7 and the middle cell is 5, so the other two cells of the top row are 3 and 7
28 = 2 x 2 x 7 has no 3, so the top-left cell is 7 and the top-right cell is 3
20 = 2 x 2 x 5 and the middle cell is 5, so the second row is 2, 5, 2
the first column is 7 x 2 x 2 = 28, so the bottom-left cell is 2
18 = 2 x 3 x 3 and the right column has 3 and 2, so the bottom-right cell is 3
4 = 2 x 2 is not a prime, so a 4 cannot sit in the grid

final_answer.spoken: the rows are seven, five, three, then two, five, two, then two, five, three

content.text:
If a number is divisible by another, the second number is called a factor of the first. For example, 4 is a factor of 12 because 12 is divisible by 4.
Prime numbers are numbers like 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, ... that have only two factors, namely 1 and themselves.
Composite numbers are numbers like 4, 6, 8, 9, ... that have more than 2 factors, i.e., at least one factor other than 1 and themselves. For example, 8 has the factor 4 and 9 has the factor 3, so 8 and 9 are both composite.
Every number greater than 1 can be written as a product of prime numbers. This is called the number's prime factorisation. For example, 84 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7.
There is only one way to factorise a number into primes, except for the ordering of the factors.
Two numbers that do not have a common factor other than 1 are said to be co-prime.
To check if two numbers are co-prime, we can first find their prime factorisations and check if there is a common prime factor. If there is no common prime factor, they are co-prime, and otherwise they are not.
A number is a factor of another number if the prime factorisation of the first number is included in the prime factorisation of the second number.

What are these numbers called? 1) Is there anything common among the shaded numbers? 2) Is there anything common among the circled numbers? 3) Which numbers are both shaded and circled? What are they called?

Book item: Yesterday, we played this game with two numbers. We ended up saying just ‘idli’ or ‘idli-vada’ and nobody said just ‘vada’! One of the numbers was 4. Oh, what could those numbers be!? Which of the following could be the other number: 2, 3, 5, 8, 10?
Book item: At what number is ‘idli-vada’ said for the 10th time?

Book item: If the game is played for the numbers 1 to 90, find out: a. How many times would the children say ‘idli’ (including the times they say ‘idli-vada’)? b. How many times would the children say ‘vada’ (including the times they say ‘idli-vada’)? c. How many times would the children say ‘idli-vada’? a) How many times would the children say ‘idli’ (including idli-vada)? b) How many times would the children say ‘vada’ (including idli-vada)? c) How many times would the children say ‘idli-vada’?
Book item: What if the game was played till 900? How would your answers change?

Book item: Is this figure (Fig. 5.1, two overlapping circles: multiples of 3 and multiples of 5, overlap labelled common multiples of 3 and 5) somehow related to the ‘idli-vada’ game? Hint: Imagine playing the game till 30. Draw the figure if the game is played till 60.
Book item: Find all multiples of 40 that lie between 310 and 410.
Book item: Find any three numbers that are multiples of 25 but not multiples of 50.

Book item: Anshu and his friends play the ‘idli-vada’ game with two numbers, which are both smaller than 10. The first time anybody says ‘idli-vada’ is after the number 50. What could the two numbers be which are assigned ‘idli’ and ‘vada’?

Book item: In the diagram below, Guna has erased all the numbers except the common multiples. Find out what those numbers could be and fill in the missing numbers in the empty regions. (Venn diagram with blank ‘Multiples of ___’ labels on both circles; the overlap shows 72, 48, 24.)
Book item: Find the smallest number that is a multiple of all the numbers from 1 to 10, except for 7.
Book item: Find the smallest number that is a multiple of all the numbers from 1 to 10.
Book item: Grumpy places a treasure on 24. Which jump sizes will get Jumpy to land on 24? (Jumpy jumps only on multiples of the jump size, starting at 0.)
Book item: Treasures are on 14 and 36 and Jumpy chooses jump size 7. He lands on 14 but not on 36. What jump size should he have chosen?
Book item: What jump size can reach both 15 and 30? There are multiple jump sizes possible. Try to find them all.

Book item: Who am I? a. I am a number less than 40. One of my factors is 7. The sum of my digits is 8. b. I am a number less than 100. Two of my factors are 3 and 5. One of my digits is 1 more than the other. a) Number less than 40, a factor is 7, digit sum 8 b) Number less than 100, factors 3 and 5, one digit is 1 more than the other

Book item: A number for which the sum of all its factors is equal to twice the number is called a perfect number. The number 28 is a perfect number. Its factors are 1, 2, 4, 7, 14 and 28. Their sum is 56 which is twice 28. Find a perfect number between 1 and 10.
Book item: Find the common factors of: a. 20 and 28, b. 35 and 50, c. 4, 8 and 12, d. 5, 15 and 25. a) 20 and 28 b) 35 and 50 c) 4, 8 and 12 d) 5, 15 and 25
Book item: In the treasure hunting game, Grumpy has kept treasures on 28 and 70. What jump sizes will land on both the numbers?

Book item: Guna wants to put 12 figs in each box and Anshu wants to put 7 figs in each box. How many arrangements are possible? Think and find out the different ways how 1. Guna can arrange 12 figs in a rectangular manner. 2. Anshu can arrange 7 figs in a rectangular manner.
Book item: Observe the number of rows and columns in each of the arrangements. How are they related to 12?
Book item: How many prime numbers are there from 21 to 30? How many composite numbers are there from 21 to 30?
Book item: We see that 2 is a prime and also an even number. Is there any other even prime?
Book item: Which of the following numbers are prime: 23, 51, 37, 26?

Book item: Identify whether each statement is true or false. Explain. a. There is no prime number whose units digit is 4. b. A product of primes can also be prime. c. Prime numbers do not have any factors. d. All even numbers are composite numbers. e. 2 is a prime and so is the next number, 3. For every other prime, the next number is composite. a) There is no prime number whose units digit is 4. b) A product of primes can also be prime. c) Prime numbers do not have any factors. d) All even numbers are composite numbers. e) 2 is a prime and so is the next number, 3. For every other prime, the next number is composite.

Book item: Can we list all the prime numbers from 1 to 100? Follow the steps: cross out 1; circle 2 and cross out its multiples; circle the next uncrossed number 3 and cross out its multiples; circle 5 and cross out its multiples; continue till all numbers are circled or crossed out.

Book item: Guna and Anshu started wondering how this simple method is able to find prime numbers! Think how this method works. Read the steps given above again and see what happens after each step is carried out.
Book item: Look at the list of primes till 100. What is the smallest difference between two successive primes? What is the largest difference?
Book item: Are there an equal number of primes occurring in every row in the table on the previous page? Which decades have the least number of primes? Which have the most number of primes?
Book item: Write three pairs of prime numbers less than 20 whose sum is a multiple of 5.
Book item: The numbers 13 and 31 are prime numbers. Both these numbers have same digits 1 and 3. Find such pairs of prime numbers up to 100.
Book item: Find seven consecutive composite numbers between 1 and 100.
Book item: Twin primes are pairs of primes having a difference of 2. For example, 3 and 5 are twin primes. So are 17 and 19. Find the other twin primes between 1 and 100.
Book item: Which of the following numbers is the product of exactly three distinct prime numbers: 45, 60, 91, 105, 330?
Book item: How many three-digit prime numbers can you make using each of 2, 4 and 5 once?
Book item: Observe that 3 is a prime number, and 2 × 3 + 1 = 7 is also a prime. Are there other primes for which doubling and adding 1 gives another prime? Find at least five such examples.

Book item: Treasures are on two numbers; Jumpy gets them only if he reaches both with the same jump size, and a jump size of 1 is not allowed. Where should Grumpy place the treasures so that Jumpy cannot reach both the treasures?
Book item: Are 15 and 39 co-prime? Are 4 and 9 co-prime?
Book item: Check if these pairs are safe: a. 15 and 39, b. 4 and 15, c. 18 and 29, d. 20 and 55 a) 15 and 39 b) 4 and 15 c) 18 and 29 d) 20 and 55

Book item: Which of the following pairs of numbers are co-prime? a. 18 and 35, b. 15 and 37, c. 30 and 415, d. 17 and 69, e. 81 and 18 a) 18 and 35 b) 15 and 37 c) 30 and 415 d) 17 and 69 e) 81 and 18

Book item: While playing the ‘idli-vada’ game with different number pairs, Anshu observed: 1. Sometimes the first common multiple was the same as the product of the two numbers. 2. At other times the first common multiple was less than the product of the two numbers. Find examples for each of the above. How is it related to the number pair being co-prime?

Book item: Teacher asks: Are 56 and 63 co-prime? Anshu writes 56 = 14 × 4 and 63 = 21 × 3 and says there are no common factors, so they are co-prime. Guna writes 56 = 7 × 8 and 63 = 9 × 7 and says 7 is a common factor, so they are not co-prime. Guna is right. But where did Anshu go wrong?

Book item: Try another example: 80 and 63. 80 = 40 × 2 = 20 × 4 = 10 × 8 = 16 × 5 = ??? and 63 = 9 × 7 = 3 × 21 = ??? Taking 80 = 16 × 5 and 63 = 9 × 7 there are no common factors. Can we conclude that 80 and 63 are co-prime?
Book item: By going through different ways of breaking down the number, we wrote 63 as 3 × 3 × 7 and as 3 × 7 × 3. Are they different?

Book item: 36 is broken in four different ways (2×18, 3×12, 4×9, 6×6) to get prime factorisations. Observe that in all four cases we get two 2s and two 3s. Multiply back to see that you get 36 in all four cases.
Book item: Using this diagram, can you explain why 30 = 2 × 3 × 5, no matter which way you multiply 2, 3, and 5?
Book item: 72 = 12 × 6. 12 = 2 × 2 × 3 and 6 = 2 × 3. Now, can you say what the prime factorisation of 72 is?
Book item: We can also write 72 as 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. Multiply and check that you get 72 back!
Book item: Observe how many times each prime factor occurs in the factorisation of 72. Compare it with how many times it occurs in the factorisations of 12 and 6 put together.
Book item: Find the prime factorisations of the following numbers: 64, 104, 105, 243, 320, 141, 1728, 729, 1024, 1331, 1000.
Book item: The prime factorisation of a number has one 2, two 3s, and one 11. What is the number?
Book item: Find three prime numbers, all less than 30, whose product is 1955.
Book item: Find the prime factorisation of these numbers without multiplying first: a. 56 × 25  b. 108 × 75  c. 1000 × 81 a) 56 × 25 b) 108 × 75 c) 1000 × 81

Book item: What is the smallest number whose prime factorisation has: a. three different prime numbers? b. four different prime numbers? a) three different prime numbers b) four different prime numbers

Book item: 80 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 5 and 63 = 3 × 3 × 7. There are no common prime factors. Can we conclude that they are co-prime? Suppose they have a common factor that is composite. Would the prime factors of this composite common factor appear in the prime factorisation of 80 and 63?
Book item: Consider 40 and 231. Their prime factorisations are 40 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 5 and 231 = 3 × 7 × 11. Are they co-prime?
Book item: Consider 242 and 195. Their prime factorisations are 242 = 2 × 11 × 11 and 195 = 3 × 5 × 13. Are they co-prime?
Book item: We say that 48 is divisible by 12 because when we divide 48 by 12, the remainder is zero. How can we check if one number is divisible by another without carrying out long division?
Book item: Is 168 divisible by 12? Find the prime factorisations of both: 168 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 and 12 = 2 × 2 × 3.
Book item: Is 75 divisible by 21? Find the prime factorisations of both: 75 = 3 × 5 × 5 and 21 = 3 × 7.
Book item: Is 42 divisible by 12? Find the prime factorisations of both: 42 = 2 × 3 × 7 and 12 = 2 × 2 × 3.

Book item: Are the following pairs of numbers co-prime? Guess first and then use prime factorisation to verify your answer. a. 30 and 45  b. 57 and 85  c. 121 and 1331  d. 343 and 216 a) 30 and 45 b) 57 and 85 c) 121 and 1331 d) 343 and 216
Book item: Is the first number divisible by the second? Use prime factorisation. a. 225 and 27  b. 96 and 24  c. 343 and 17  d. 999 and 99 a) 225 and 27 b) 96 and 24 c) 343 and 17 d) 999 and 99
Book item: The first number has prime factorisation 2 × 3 × 7 and the second number has prime factorisation 3 × 7 × 11. Are they co-prime? Does one of them divide the other?
Book item: Guna says, "Any two prime numbers are co-prime?". Is he right?

objectives.objective_text: Students list the multiples of 3 and of 5 by skip counting and use them to say which numbers get idli and which get vada.
Students find the numbers that are multiples of both numbers in a game, name them common multiples, and spot them on a table or a two-circle figure.
Students decide which number pairs give idli or idli-vada but never just vada, and explain that every multiple of the larger number must be a multiple of the smaller.
Students call the idli-vada game for chosen number pairs on the tool, find the common multiples and predict the first one before it comes.
Students find every jump size that lands on a treasure number, include 1 and the number itself, and call these jump sizes the factors of the number.
Students find the jump sizes that reach two treasures by listing the factors of each number and picking the numbers in both lists.
Students place treasures on the tool, list the factors of one number and the common factors of two, and find numbers from clues about their factors and multiples.
Students list every rectangle that 12 figs and 7 figs can make, and see that 12 has several and 7 has only one.
Students connect the rows and columns of each rectangle to the factors of the number and explain why a number with only one rectangle has just two factors.
Students call a number with exactly two factors prime, one with more composite, say why 1 is neither, and count the primes between 21 and 30.
Students lay out dot rectangles on the tool to find factors, tag numbers as prime, composite or neither, and judge statements about primes.
Students follow the five steps of the sieve on a table of 1 to 100 and list the primes they find, crossing out 1 first and multiples of each circled number.
Students explain why a number left uncrossed has no smaller factor, so it is prime, and why every crossed number is composite.
Students run the sieve on the tool, read off primes, and use the list of primes to answer questions about gaps, twins and consecutive composites.
Students choose two treasure numbers that Jumpy cannot reach by a jump size above 1, and call such pairs, with only 1 as a common factor, co-prime.
Students list the factors of both numbers in each pair, look for a common factor other than 1, and decide whether the pair is co-prime.
Students compare the first common multiple of a pair with the product of the pair, and see that the two are equal exactly when the pair is co-prime.
Students draw thread art on the tool for chosen peg counts and gaps, and link whether the thread reaches every peg to the pair being co-prime.
Students explain why writing 56 as 14 times 4 does not show all the factors of 56, and why a systematic way of checking factors is needed.
Students write a number as a product of primes, see that different ways of splitting give the same primes in the same counts, and that the order of multiplying does not matter.
Students find the prime factorisation of a product by putting together the factorisations of its two factors, and check by multiplying back.
Students split numbers into factor trees on the tool, compare different trees of one number, and write prime factorisations, even of products, without multiplying first.
Students write two numbers as products of primes and conclude they are co-prime when no prime appears in both, giving the reason.
Students check whether one number divides another by seeing whether the prime factorisation of the second number sits inside that of the first.
Students compare the prime factorisations of two numbers on the tool and decide whether they are co-prime and whether one divides the other.
Students list the multiples of 10, see that all end in 0, and decide whether a number such as 125 or 8560 is divisible by 10 from its last digit alone.
Students list the multiples of 5, notice that the last digit is 0 or 5, and use it to test any number for divisibility by 5.
Students list the multiples of 2, notice the last digit is 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8, and use it to test a number for divisibility by 2.
Students test numbers for 10, 5 and 2 with the last digit on the tool, check by division, and find remainders from the last digit.
Students list the multiples of 4, test whether the last digit decides divisibility, and see with 12 and 22 that it does not.
Students list multiples of 4 in different hundreds and thousands, and see that the last two digits stay multiples of 4, so 100 does not change divisibility.
Students test numbers for divisibility by 4 using the last two digits, and judge three statements about the rule with examples.
Students use the lens on the tool to test numbers for 4, apply the rule to leap years and palindromes, and explore even and odd sums.
Students test whether the last two digits decide divisibility by 8 by comparing numbers that end in the same two digits, and see that they do not.
Students list multiples of 8 in different thousands, see that the last three digits repeat, and state the rule that the last three digits decide divisibility by 8.
Students change the last digits of a number to make it divisible by 8 and judge statements about the last-three-digits rule.
Students combine the tests for 2, 4, 5, 8 and 10 to check large numbers with the fewest tests, and build numbers with a given product.
Students read the classmates' reasons for the box 9, 16, 25, 43, check each against all four numbers, and find that one number can be special for more than one reason.
Students look at four numbers in each box, name how each is special compared to the rest with factors, multiples and primes, and check the reasons they give are true for that number only.
Students work out the rules of the grid puzzle from a solved example and follow a solved puzzle in which every row and column multiplies to its clue.
Students solve harder grids by breaking each clue into primes and checking every row and column product.
Students fill 3 by 3 grids with primes by breaking each clue into primes and matching every row and column product.
Students restate what factors, primes, composites, co-primes and prime factorisation are, and how prime factorisation checks co-primes and divisibility.
